lead: Digital passband modulation puts bits onto a carrier that can travel through a cable or air. Binary ASK changes carrier amplitude; this chapter studies the zero-level form, OOK: bit 1 is a carrier burst and bit 0 is silence. Binary ASK can also use two nonzero amplitudes. BFSK changes carrier frequency between two tones. The receiver knows the bit clock and uses a matched filter or correlator to decide each bit in noise. These schemes are simple and cheap, so they appear in remote keyless entry, RFID readers, low-rate telemetry and older telephone modems. This chapter shows generation, coherent detection, bandwidth and bit error probability for binary ASK and binary FSK.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 complex envelope and AWGN, and Unit 5 matched filter and signal space (see Unit 5, Matched filter and correlation receiver).

blocks.where: A is carrier amplitude in volts; b(t) is 1 or 0 during a bit; f<sub>c</sub> is carrier frequency in hertz; T<sub>b</sub> is bit duration in seconds.

blocks.text: Generation uses a multiplier (balanced modulator) or a switch. The NRZ data has levels 0 and 1. The switch passes the carrier for 1 and blocks it for 0; a multiplier gives cleaner multiplication.

Coherent detection multiplies the received signal by 2cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) and integrates over one bit T<sub>b</sub>. For bit 1 the correlator output is A T<sub>b</sub>; for bit 0 it is 0. The threshold is A T<sub>b</sub>/2. The factor 2 cancels the 1/2 from cos².

For equiprobable bits, peak carrier power is A²/2 W, average signal power is A²/4 W, and average bit energy is E<sub>b</sub> = A²T<sub>b</sub>/4 J. The null-to-null bandwidth is 2R<sub>b</sub>, where R<sub>b</sub> = 1/T<sub>b</sub> is the bit rate.
BFSK sends bit 1 as frequency f<sub>1</sub> (mark) and bit 0 as f<sub>0</sub> (space), both with amplitude A:
s<sub>1</sub>(t) = A cos(2πf<sub>1</sub>t), s<sub>0</sub>(t) = A cos(2πf<sub>0</sub>t)
blocks.where: f<sub>1</sub> is mark frequency; f<sub>0</sub> is space frequency; both in hertz; A is amplitude in volts.

blocks.text: Generation uses a voltage-controlled oscillator whose frequency shifts with the input voltage, or two switched oscillators. Switching can cause phase jumps; continuous-phase FSK avoids them, as in MSK (see 6.6).
Coherent detection uses two correlators, one at f<sub>0</sub> and one at f<sub>1</sub>. Each multiplies by 2cos and integrates over T<sub>b</sub>. The larger output wins.
Tones are coherently orthogonal over Tb when the spacing is n/(2Tb) for integer n; the minimum is 1/(2Tb) = Rb/2. Noncoherent detection needs spacing 1/Tb (see 6.3).

blocks.where: Δf is frequency deviation in hertz; R<sub>b</sub> = 1/T<sub>b</sub> is bit rate in bits per second; h is modulation index; B is Carson bandwidth in hertz.

blocks.text: The ASK power spectral density has a carrier line and sinc² lobes around f<sub>c</sub>. Its first nulls are at f<sub>c</sub> ± R<sub>b</sub>, so the null-to-null bandwidth is 2R<sub>b</sub>. The BFSK spectrum is the sum of two such lobes at f<sub>0</sub> and f<sub>1</sub>; Carson bandwidth 2(Δf + R<sub>b</sub>) contains most of the power.
For coherent OOK and coherent orthogonal BFSK in AWGN, the bit error probability is

blocks.where: P<sub>b</sub> is bit error probability; E<sub>b</sub> is average bit energy in joules; N<sub>0</sub> is one-sided noise power spectral density in W/Hz; Q(x) = ∫<sub>x</sub><sup>∞</sup> (1/√(2π)) e<sup>−u²/2</sup> du.

blocks.text: For BFSK E<sub>b</sub> = A²T<sub>b</sub>/2. For equiprobable OOK average E<sub>b</sub> = A²T<sub>b</sub>/4. BFSK is constant envelope, so a nonlinear power amplifier can be used. OOK average power is half its peak.

figure.caption: The data bit stream becomes NRZ; one branch multiplies it by a carrier for ASK, the other switches between 100 kHz and 110 kHz tones for FSK. The coherent detector uses a matched filter to output bits.

spec.title: ASK and FSK: generation and coherent detection
spec.aria: Binary data branches to an ASK multiplier and an FSK switch, then passes through a channel and a coherent detector to output bits.

examples.question: A binary FSK transmitter sends data at R<sub>b</sub> = 10 kbps. The mark frequency is 100 kHz and the space frequency is 110 kHz. Find the frequency deviation Δf, the modulation index h, the Carson bandwidth, and the minimum coherent tone spacing for orthogonality. State whether the actual tones are orthogonal.
steps: Tone spacing = |110 − 100| kHz = 10 kHz. Frequency deviation Δf = spacing/2 = 5 kHz = 5000 Hz.
Carson bandwidth B = 2(Δf + R<sub>b</sub>) = 2(5 + 10) kHz = 30 kHz = 30,000 Hz.
Minimum coherent spacing = 1/(2T<sub>b</sub>) = R<sub>b</sub>/2 = 10 kbps/2 = 5 kHz = 5000 Hz.

Actual spacing = 10 kHz = 2 × 5 kHz = 2(R<sub>b</sub>/2), so n = 2. Therefore the tones are orthogonal. Being merely above the minimum does not guarantee orthogonality; the spacing must equal nR<sub>b</sub>/2 for a positive integer n.
examples.answer: Δf = 5 kHz, h = 1, Carson bandwidth = 30 kHz, minimum coherent spacing = 5 kHz; actual spacing 10 kHz = 2(R<sub>b</sub>/2), n = 2, so the tones are orthogonal.
examples.check:
R_b = 10_000
f_mark = 100_000
f_space = 110_000
spacing = abs(f_space - f_mark)
delta_f = spacing / 2
h = 2 * delta_f / R_b
bandwidth = 2 * (delta_f + R_b)
T_b = 1 / R_b
min_spacing = 1 / (2 * T_b)
print(delta_f)
print(h)
print(bandwidth)
print(min_spacing)
print(spacing)

traps: In B = 2(Δf + R<sub>b</sub>), R<sub>b</sub> is bits per second, not T<sub>b</sub> seconds. Substituting T<sub>b</sub> breaks the units.
Δf is half the tone spacing. For 100 kHz and 110 kHz, Δf = 5 kHz, not 10 kHz. Then h = 2Δf/R<sub>b</sub>.

BFSK needs two tones. Coherent orthogonality requires spacing = nR<sub>b</sub>/2 for positive integer n (minimum R<sub>b</sub>/2 when n = 1); noncoherent orthogonality requires spacing = nR<sub>b</sub> (minimum R<sub>b</sub> when n = 1). Zero spacing is not orthogonal. A spacing merely above the minimum is not automatically orthogonal.
For equiprobable OOK, average power is A²/4 W, half the peak A²/2 W. Using peak power doubles E<sub>b</sub> and gives the wrong Q argument.
Coherent detection needs a phase-locked local carrier. Envelope detection is noncoherent; see 6.3.

quiz.a: Binary ASK in which bit 1 is a carrier burst and bit 0 is no carrier.

quiz.q: State the BFSK modulation index in words and symbols.
quiz.a: h = 2Δf/R<sub>b</sub>, where Δf is half the tone spacing and R<sub>b</sub> is bit rate.

quiz.q: Why is the coherent OOK threshold A T<sub>b</sub>/2?
quiz.a: The correlator output is A T<sub>b</sub> for 1 and 0 for 0; the midpoint minimises errors for equal probabilities.

quiz.q: A BFSK link sends 20 kbps with tones at 200 kHz and 210 kHz. Find Δf, h, Carson bandwidth, and minimum coherent spacing.
quiz.a: Spacing = 10 kHz, Δf = 5 kHz, h = 2×5/20 = 0.5, B = 2(5+20) = 50 kHz, minimum spacing = R<sub>b</sub>/2 = 10 kHz. The actual spacing equals the minimum, so the tones are orthogonal.

quiz.q: An OOK transmitter has A = 2 V and T<sub>b</sub> = 1 ms with equiprobable bits. Find peak power, average power, and average E<sub>b</sub>.
quiz.a: Peak power = A²/2 = 2 W. Average power = A²/4 = 1 W. Average E<sub>b</sub> = 1 W × 1 ms = 1 mJ.

quiz.q: Why does BFSK usually need more bandwidth than ASK for the same bit rate?
quiz.a: ASK has one carrier and null-to-null bandwidth 2R<sub>b</sub>. BFSK has two tones and Carson bandwidth 2(Δf+R<sub>b</sub>). The tone spacing adds 2Δf, so BFSK is wider unless Δf is very small, which loses orthogonality.

beyond: Not for the exam. ASK remains common in optical links and simple 433 MHz modules because a switch is enough. Bluetooth basic rate uses GFSK, a filtered FSK, to keep the spectrum narrow. Software-defined radios demodulate FSK by quadrature mixing and digital filters. Search next: GFSK, orthogonal FSK, noncoherent FSK detection.
